The Trip

Eight nights, three beach days, and no airport

You drive to the pier. That's the whole travel day.

Most Bahamas cruises leave from Florida. This one leaves from Galveston — about a four-hour drive from Houston, no flights, no baggage fees, no 4:30 a.m. TSA line. You park the car and you're on the ship.

Eight nights, four of them at sea, and three Bahamas beach days back to back: Nassau on Tuesday, Half Moon Cay on Wednesday, Celebration Key on Thursday. Two of the three are private destinations where your ship is essentially the only crowd on the sand. The sea days are spent on a 2023-built Excel-class ship with a roller coaster on the top deck and ten restaurants — full details further down if you want them.

7C Cove Balcony Stateroom
Deck 5  ·  Midship  ·  Sleeps Four

A cove balcony isn't a smaller version of a regular balcony — it's a different thing. Rather than hanging off the side of the ship behind a glass rail, it sits recessed into the hull itself, framed by solid steel on the sides and up to about waist height. Deck 5 is the lowest balcony deck on Jubilee, which puts you close enough to the water to hear it.

The trade is straightforward. You give up the wide-open view and the elevated vantage in port. You get real privacy — nobody above or beside you can see in, which is not true of a standard balcony — plus shelter from wind and the sea at eye level instead of from six decks up. In heavy weather expect some spray, and on rare occasions these balconies are closed for safety.

Nassau, The Bahamas

Tuesday, July 13 · 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

Nassau is the only stop on this sailing that is an actual city — a working capital with traffic, government buildings, and a downtown that existed for two hundred years before cruise ships showed up. You dock at Prince George Wharf and walk straight into it.

Bay Street starts at the pier: straw market, jewelry shops, rum cake by the box. Two blocks uphill you hit the Queen's Staircase, sixty-five steps cut by hand out of solid limestone in the late 1700s, and Fort Fincastle at the top with the best free view on the island. That's a comfortable ninety-minute loop on foot.

For a real Nassau afternoon, head west about fifteen minutes to Arawak Cay — locals call it the Fish Fry. It's a strip of pastel-painted shacks serving conch salad chopped to order in front of you, cracked conch, and Kalik beer. Not a tourist recreation; just where people eat.

Advisor Note With a 5:00 p.m. departure you have a genuinely full day here — long enough for a beach club, a boat excursion, and lunch. It's the one port where booking something in advance is worth it, because the walk-up options at the pier are the most expensive and the most crowded.

RelaxAway, Half Moon Cay

Wednesday, July 14 · 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

A 2,400-acre private island sitting between Eleuthera and Cat Island, roughly a hundred miles southeast of Nassau. For nearly thirty years there was no pier here — every guest arrived by tender, and the size of those boats quietly capped how many people could stand on the sand at once. That's what made it beloved and that's what made it small.

The pier opened in June 2026. Jubilee is an Excel-class ship, which means you now walk off directly instead of queuing for a tender at 7:00 a.m. — a meaningful change if you have anyone in the group who doesn't love standing in a line to get on a small boat.

The north side is the new Carnival half: a tram running six stops, cabanas along the water, two lunch venues, and a set of beach bars. The south end stays quieter — that's Holland America's traditional side and the stretch of crescent beach the island built its reputation on. Water here is shallow and glass-clear a long way out, which is the whole reason people rank this above most Caribbean beaches.

Advisor Note Cabanas and the horseback ride into the water are the two things that sell out first on this island, and they sell out weeks ahead, not days. If either is on your list, that's an early decision rather than a day-of one.

Celebration Key, Grand Bahama

Thursday, July 15 · 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

The newest thing in the Bahamas and the most deliberately engineered. Celebration Key opened on the east end of Grand Bahama in July 2025 on a $600 million build — not a natural island but a purpose-made shore day, laid out in five distinct areas so a family of five can split up and still meet for lunch.

Starfish Lagoon is the family end, built around the largest freshwater lagoon in the Caribbean. Suncastle is the ten-story sandcastle-shaped tower with waterslides running out of it. Calypso Lagoon is the livelier side with a swim-up bar and a floating stage. Pearl Cove Beach Club is adults-only, an infinity pool facing open water, and it carries a separate charge. Lokono Cove is the retail and crafts portal, named through a community competition on Grand Bahama, and it's also where you exit if you want to see the actual island beyond the resort.

The pier was doubled to four berths in 2026, so plan on this being the busiest of your three beach days — more ships, more people, more infrastructure to absorb them.

Advisor Note The 4:00 p.m. departure is an hour earlier than the other two ports. If you want Pearl Cove, book it before you sail — it's capacity-controlled and it is the one part of Celebration Key that consistently sells out at sea.

Four Days at Sea

Days 2, 3, 7 and 8

Two out, two back. On a smaller ship four sea days would be a lot. On a 182,800-ton Excel-class ship it's the reason to book an eight-night instead of a seven.

Practically: sea days are when the specialty restaurants have availability, when the spa runs its lowest pricing, when you can get a good chair without setting an alarm — and when the ship's programming is at full throttle. Dive-In Movies run on the big screen at the Carnival Seaside Theater after dark, which on a warm Gulf night with the pool still open is the easiest night of the trip.

Jubilee is the third of Carnival's Excel-class ships, following Mardi Gras and Carnival Celebration, and it's the one that got the two new zones. Instead of one long promenade, the ship is divided into six areas with distinct looks and their own bars and restaurants — the idea being that you move between them across a day rather than parking in one spot.

Grand Central

The three-deck atrium, and the design move that defines the ship — floor-to-ceiling windows facing the ocean instead of an interior light well. JavaBlue Cafe, Bonsai Sushi and Bonsai Teppanyaki all sit here.

Currents

One of two zones new to Jubilee. Home to Dr. Inks, Ph.D. — a cephalopod-themed bar that is exactly as odd as it sounds — and The Golden Mermaid.

The Shores

The second new zone, built as a coastal-boardwalk stretch of casual food and open-air seating.

French Quarter

New Orleans by way of the Gulf: live jazz most nights, Emeril Lagasse's bistro, and Fahrenheit 555 steakhouse nearby.

Summer Landing & Lido

The pool decks. WaterWorks slides, the Carnival Seaside Theater screen, mini golf routed past cacti and windmills, and the Havana Bar for a quieter Cuban-styled corner.

BOLT: Ultimate Sea Coaster

A roller coaster on the top deck, 187 feet above the water. Separate charge, worth doing once, best at sunset.

Specialty dining, BOLT, spa services, and Pearl Cove Beach Club at Celebration Key all carry separate charges and are not included in your cruise fare. Jubilee is wheelchair accessible; designated smoking areas exist onboard, and all dining venues are non-smoking.

Included in your fare

  • Eight nights aboard Carnival Jubilee
  • Main dining room service, buffet, and the complimentary casual venues — Guy's Burger Joint, BlueIguana Cantina, Street Eats, Big Chicken, pizza and deli around the clock
  • Room service breakfast and the complimentary overnight menu
  • All entertainment: production shows, live music across the zones, comedy club, Seaside Theater films
  • Pools, WaterWorks slides, mini golf, sports deck, fitness center
  • Camp Ocean youth programming by age group
  • All government taxes, fees, and port expenses
  • All three Bahamas port calls

Not included

  • Gratuities — charged daily to your onboard account and prepayable before sailing
  • Beverage packages, individual bar drinks, bottled water, specialty coffee
  • Specialty restaurants: Fahrenheit 555, Rudi's Seagrill, Emeril's bistro, Cucina del Capitano, Bonsai Teppanyaki, ChiBang!
  • BOLT roller coaster and other pay-per-use attractions
  • Shore excursions, cabanas, and Pearl Cove Beach Club at Celebration Key
  • Cloud 9 Spa treatments, Wi-Fi plans, casino, photos
  • Travel insurance
  • Parking at the Galveston terminal
Documents: All U.S. citizens on a closed-loop sailing from Galveston need a valid passport book or, at minimum, an original birth certificate plus a government photo ID. A passport is strongly recommended — if anyone has to leave the ship unexpectedly from a foreign port, it's the difference between a flight home and a consulate appointment. Passports should be valid at least six months past July 18, 2027.

Optional — Complimentary Hold

Want me to hold a stateroom while you decide?

I can place a courtesy hold on a specific cabin at no cost and no obligation, which keeps it off the market while you talk it over. To do that the cruise line needs each traveler's full legal name exactly as it appears on their passport or birth certificate, plus date of birth.

Getting these right now also saves a step later — a misspelled name on a booking is corrected by the cruise line, sometimes with a fee, and always slowly. Nicknames, middle-name-as-first-name, and hyphen differences are the usual culprits.
